items.title: EXCLUSIVE: Rubio warns top staff against conflicts of interest as Republicans look to 2028
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has moved to tighten control over the State Department, telling senior officials that staff must stay in their lanes and avoid actions that present conflicts of interest, four people familiar with the matter said.

Rubio's message, delivered in a meeting last week before the Republican Party's electoral losses on Tuesday, comes as its leading figures attempt to put distance between themselves and an increasingly unpopular Trump administration.

The meeting followed the high-profile resignation of US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle in mid-October after news reports raised concerns that she sold access to Trump administration officials in exchange for money, gifts and favors.

Guilfoyle has called the reports false and in a post on social media said she would defend her reputation.

Rubio told the meeting, which included many of the roughly two dozen assistant secretaries of state, that unethical behavior would result in a firing, regardless of how well-connected an official might be, said one of the people.

He added that too many officials were making decisions or pushing policy agendas without coordinating and that significant decisions required his signoff or that of Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Details of the meeting have not previously been reported.

The State Department declined to comment on the meeting.

Soon after the meeting, three of the people said, the State Department's policy chief, Jeremy Lewin, was forced out of his job in part due to concerns that he was working on matters outside his area without proper coordination. The exact details of those concerns remain unclear.

None of the people who spoke to Reuters suggested Lewin's departure was linked to any incidents of ethical misconduct. Lewin joined the government as part of Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency and helped dismantle the US Agency for International Development, which oversaw US foreign assistance.

Rubio and others within the State Department leadership were frustrated with his "freelancing" and going against "certain directives from the Secretary," one of the people said, without providing specific examples.

Lewin, who was appointed to his senior role just over two months ago, said on social media last month that he had stepped down from his role to return to the private sector.

Asked for comment, a State Department official said: "It was mutually agreed it was time (for Lewin) to move on."

Lewin said in a statement to Reuters that his departure was planned several weeks before it was announced and he denied he was fired.

"The suggestion that I was fired is false. As planned for weeks with the Secretary and his team, after staying longer than expected to finish key projects, I resigned my position prior to the midterms to assume a private sector role and plan my wedding," he said.

"It had nothing to do with any meeting or policy regarding the management of the department."

Rubio's frustrations also included excessive overseas travel by political staff, which has led to a requirement that Rubio's office approve all political travel, according to another one of the people.

REPUBLICANS LOOK BEYOND MIDTERM LOSSES

The 2028 presidential race began shifting into gear almost immediately after Tuesday's midterm elections delivered control of Congress to the Democrats. Vice President JD Vance and Republican Senator Ted Cruz offered post-mortems on X that many strategists saw as political vision statements as the campaign season begins.

Rubio himself has sought to play down reports that he is considering a run, but he has also not publicly ruled it out. If he does, his management of the State Department could emerge as a topic of conversation on the campaign trail.

President Donald Trump's administration has faced consistent accusations of self-dealing and Democrats have said they will put dealings between Trump aides and foreign officials under the microscope when they take control of Congress in January and begin launching official investigations.

The Trump administration has denied allegations of self-dealing.

Shortly after Guilfoyle left the administration in October, Rubio sent a department-wide memo reminding diplomats to "avoid conflicts of interest," according to multiple media outlets.

He subsequently denied that the memo was sent as a result of Guilfoyle's departure, telling reporters that he had in fact meant to send it weeks earlier, but that it had been held up for bureaucratic reasons.

Like other parts of the Trump administration, Rubio's department has lost officials recently.

In October, US Special Representative for Global Partnerships Paolo Zampolli was fired after Politico reported an email thread between him and Landau, in which Landau accused Zampolli of working outside his "lane" of cultural diplomacy, saying Zampolli kept wanting to work on issues outside his remit in contravention of Landau's orders.

Reuters could not determine what those issues were.

Shortly after his departure, Zampolli wrote on X that special envoy appointments last one year by statute and that Trump had extended his appointment by more than six months.

items.title: After midterm rout, Vance tries to build his own 2028 brand
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Late in his blitz to salvage Republicans' midterm fortunes, Vice President JD Vance shifted strategy. He talked less about President Donald Trump and more about the issues that define his own political identity.

Vance argued the case for Republicans, who lost control of Congress in Tuesday's vote, almost exclusively through the lens of his policy portfolio, according to a Reuters review of half a dozen speeches since the Republican convention in September.

He bypassed Trump's signature policies including the Iran war and deportations as polls showed the president's sagging popularity dragging down Republican office-seekers.

The change was deliberate, according to two people familiar with the strategy. Vance and his advisers saw the issues he championed — economic nationalism, foreign policy restraint, and public safety — as politically potent subjects he could address with authority. While Trump embraced them as part of his MAGA movement, Vance had emerged as their lead crusader, the people said.

The shift offered an early glimpse of how the 42-year-old vice president could chart his own course as Republicans begin looking beyond Trump.

Vance hasn't said whether he will run for president in 2028, and Trump hasn't endorsed him or anyone else. But Vance is viewed as a leading potential contender who some Republican officials say will need to inherit much of Trump's coalition while separating himself from his boss's baggage.

Vance took a more public step on Wednesday toward reinforcing his own political brand with an unusually blunt election postmortem. In a social media post, he blamed the Iran war for Republicans' midterm defeat and laid out a platform for a Republican rebound.

He called for a swift end to the conflict and urged Republicans to focus on affordability, reevaluate foreign relations and overhaul the US relationship with Israel.

Trump has called Americans' affordability concerns a Democratic "hoax." He launched a war against Iran following sustained lobbying from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump went on to endorse Netanyahu in the Israeli election.

VANCE MAKES UNEASE AT THE WAR PUBLIC

The post for the first time put Vance openly on the side of ending the war.

Three people familiar with the White House and Vance's communications told Reuters that the vice president was not breaking with Trump and said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles knew in advance about Vance's post.

On Friday, Trump reshuffled senior White House leadership, replacing Wiles with Stephen Miller in a move that suggests the White House plans to double down on some of Trump's more hardline policies.

Trump has acknowledged the Iran war played a role in the Republican rout because of the resulting high gas prices but has continued to defend it. "I would have done nothing different," he told reporters on Wednesday.

Reuters could not determine whether Trump was aware of the post in advance.

Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son, endorsed Vance's remarks on social media, along with some conservative allies.

The dialogue further elevated Vance as a potential post-Trump conservative standard-bearer, said Michael Ricci, a Republican strategist and former adviser to House Speakers John Boehner and Paul Ryan.

USING THE MEGAPHONE OF THE VICE PRESIDENCY

He said Vance's message forced conservatives to debate the merits of the war, and more broadly, what core tenets Republican presidential candidates should embrace in 2028.

"It's simplistic to say this about him looking for ways to differentiate himself from Trump," Ricci said. "This is about him using his megaphone of the vice presidency to set the terms of debate."

Representatives for Vance declined to comment. White House representatives referred Reuters to Trump's comments on Wednesday, when he told reporters he understood Vance's perspective on the election results.

Democrats are poised to tie Vance – or any Republican nominee – to Trump in 2028, especially if Trump plays a large role in vetting conservative hopefuls.

"There's a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring," said Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist.

Vance's brand did not emerge from the midterms unscathed. Republicans lost in states where he campaigned. Some of the strategies he endorsed – including an ad by Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that cast doubt on the sexual abuse suffered by the victorious Democratic candidate, Amy Acton – may have swung races away from Republicans.

Other possible 2028 presidential contenders have offered their diagnoses of the midterm defeat. US Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said Republicans hadn't done enough on affordability. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said losing candidates had focused too heavily on transgender issues and neglected voter concerns about data centers and artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has stayed silent.

Vance's effort to shape the debate was visible during the closing days of the campaign.

In stump speeches, he told voters to support Republicans because they would investigate fraud in federal health care and antipoverty programs, tying that to the White House's immigration agenda and cost of living. He almost entirely ignored the Iran war and gas prices, and seldom mentioned Trump by name.

"I want my kids to raise a family in a country that is vibrant and thriving and free and prosperous. I want the simple things," Vance told one of his final rallies in North Carolina. "And because I want that for me, I want it for you too."

items.title: Cornell faculty senate declares no confidence in university leadership
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Cornell University's faculty senate approved a resolution of no confidence on Friday in the administration's ability to handle what it has called a sexual assault crisis, after a former student sued the university for not protecting her from an alleged 2024 gang rape.

The resolution, which 55.6% of elected faculty senators who cast votes supported, is a condemnation of Cornell's leadership from its major legislative and advisory body, but has no concrete consequences. The tally showed 37% voted against it and 7.4% abstained, Cornell University spokesperson Rebecca Valli said.

"The Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University," the resolution said.

The former student, who is identified by the pseudonym Jane Doe in court documents, alleged in her civil complaint that Cornell failed to protect her from being raped.

Her lawsuit, filed in September, has also drawn criticism of the university's handling of the case in 2024. Cornell, located in Ithaca, New York, responded that it had conducted a comprehensive investigation and imposed disciplinary measures, including expulsions.

BOARD SUPPORTS PRESIDENT

In response to the resolution, Cornell University Board Chair Anne Smalling expressed the board of trustees' support for University President Michael Kotlikoff and the administration.

"Today's Faculty Senate vote reflects the deep anger across our campus and sends a clear signal that what happened to Jane Doe is unacceptable," the statement said. "We support President Kotlikoff's commitment to taking all necessary steps to ensure students are safe on campus and working together as a community to help prevent this from happening again."

Kotlikoff has not responded to the university about the vote outcome, Valli, the university spokesperson, said. Under university procedures, the president has 30 days to respond in writing, she said.

Kotlikoff said the day before voting began on October 29 that faculty discussion and debate were "an important component of Cornell's shared governance" and that the university had taken measures including adding staff to its civil rights office, expanding sexual assault prevention education, and hiring staff focused on victim advocacy.

Cornell faculty senator Risa Lieberwitz, who co-sponsored the resolution, has said the administration failed to address the sexual assault problem in a systemic way during the more than a decade Kotlikoff has served in senior leadership. Kotlikoff has been Cornell president since March last year.

"Students, faculty, and staff have lost trust that sexual assault cases will be handled properly," Lieberwitz said in an online discussion of the resolution on the Cornell website in late October. "This will have a chilling effect on reporting, creating fear that reporting sexual assault to this administration will be ineffective and even damaging."

Dean of Faculty Chris Schaffer had previously said in a post that he opposed the resolution because it did not "articulate the specific failures underlying its judgment or the consequences it seeks."

"When we make a judgment this consequential, we should state clearly what has failed and what we expect to change," he wrote. "This resolution falls short of that standard."

In a separate post ahead of the vote, Schaffer said that passage of a no confidence resolution would result in "no binding consequence."

items.title: In Republican collapse, Colorado military town elects Democrat for the first time
items.content_html:
COLORADO SPRINGS, Colorado, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Colorado Springs, a military town and global center for Christian evangelism, has sent a Republican to Washington every election since its US House of Representatives district was created in 1970.

Then came 2026.

The victory of Jessica Killin, an Army veteran who was among dozens of Democrats who flipped a seat this week, is one of the starkest examples of how the party built its resounding win on affordability issues, demographics and candidates, one district at a time.

In an area with five military installations, where soldiers pack fast-food restaurants at lunchtime, Killin's triumph relied on votes of veterans, service members and their families, who represent about a third of the population, and for whom the war in Iran is personal. A soldier deployed from the city's Fort Carson US Army base was among the first Americans to die in the conflict.

Killin, a first-time candidate, said her win was a repudiation of Republican incumbent Jeff Crank's support for President Donald Trump and underscored voters' frustrations with the Iran war, tariffs and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

A supporter who canvassed for her found immigration also was on the minds of Latinos in a district where the population of metropolitan Colorado Springs more than doubled to around 782,000 in the last four decades, bringing greater ethnic diversity and a younger, more highly educated electorate.

"I am resolved to make the history that really matters, combating horrific corruption and chaos that we are all honestly sick of in Washington, DC," Killin, a former US Army paratrooper and aide to ex-second gentleman Doug Emhoff, told reporters on Thursday.

Crank had tried to portray Killin as an outsider.

"We cannot let our community turn into Denver or Boulder," Crank posted on social media last week, referring to the two Democratic-controlled cities to the north.

Killin targeted centrist and left-leaning residents in the state's second-largest city, and her hometown, who in the past three presidential cycles abandoned both major parties, swelling unaffiliated voters by nearly half to 53% of the electorate in El Paso County, according to county data.

In a metropolitan area where more than 200 space, aerospace, cybersecurity, and defense companies employ around 111,000 people, and account for over 40% of the local economy, Killin hammered Crank's support of Trump's "reckless" war in Iran and argued that Congress needed to reclaim its war-powers authority.

Karl Schneider, 57, a former US special forces officer and ex-vice chairman of the El Paso Republican Party, backed Killin to rein in a presidency he sees as militarily out of control.

"Donald Trump is a clear and present danger to the United States of America, our republic, and I think to the rest of the world," said Schneider, an executive at an AI cybersecurity advisory firm who served as a US Army Green Beret.

For Republican voter Rick Wood, 67, Crank failed to help tackle high gas and grocery prices and tied himself too closely to Trump, whose approval rating is near a career low of 32%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos national poll.

"They ran on Trump's coattails," said Wood, a US Air Force veteran.

'NEVER SEEN BEFORE'

Some Republicans interviewed by Reuters in the district that is home to the Focus on the Family evangelical organization were stunned by the blue wave, saying they feared the country would descend into communism, echoing warnings from Trump about the recent rise of left-wing Democratic candidates.

Politics professor Sara Hagedorn saw Killin, and other Democrats who won in former Republican strongholds, as a possible return to the fiscally responsible "Blue Dog" Democrats of the 1990s and early 2000s who worked across party lines.

"She has a real opportunity here to be a real moderate or independent voice within the Democratic Party," said Hagedorn, who teaches at the University of Colorado, Colorado Springs.

Killin's campaign coffers swelled after the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee listed the district as "in play" in February, the first time the committee had targeted the area.

Bruce Barron, 65, a former Republican congressional aide, canvassed for Killin in southeast Colorado Springs where the school district has around 54% Hispanic students and many of the Black community live.

"Every Hispanic I talked to, it resonates with them, the concern about Hispanics not being safe under the Trump administration," said Barron.

Killin's campaign outraised Crank's by nearly two to one with $5.6 million in funds. Crank received $5.8 million in outside spending, giving the two similar war chests.

Killin deployed over 400 volunteers to knock on over 100,000 doors while hosting around 150 events to meet voters, according to her campaign.

As Kyle Ries, 40, canvassed for Killin in south Colorado Springs, where American flags fly outside many homes and fuel-hungry pickups stand in driveways, he met conservatives willing to support Killin after they saw Crank back a war that has stoked energy prices.

"This is a candidate that this district has never seen before," Ries, an IT professional, said of Killin.

Reporting by Andrew Hay in Colorado Springs and Brad Brooks in Longmont. Editing by Donna Bryson and Alistair Bell

items.title: White House recasts Trump arch as military tribute
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Hours after a US judge paused construction on President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot (76.2-meter) arch in Washington, the White House on Friday shared new depictions portraying the project as a tribute to the nation's military heritage, the latest attempt to rebrand it amid mounting opposition.

The site unveiled on Friday calls the project, which would stand near the entrance of Arlington National Cemetery, the Military Triumphal Arch.

Animated images show a trio of gilded, winged statues above the words "GOLDEN AGE OF AMERICA," written in gold letters set against stone. A flame emanates from a torch in the hands of one of the winged female figures.

The White House shared the new renderings from a group called the United States Triumphal Arch Foundation. The group's chairman, former Trump-appointed ambassador Randy Evans, said in a statement that the foundation is not connected to the government.

Trump has increasingly turned his attention to a series of major projects in Washington, both before and after his Republican Party suffered massive losses in Tuesday's midterm elections that cost the party control of Congress.

The arch and Trump's other signature projects have drawn significant political and legal opposition.

The attorneys general from Virginia and the District of Columbia have sued to prevent construction of the arch, which they say will irreparably damage the skyline of the nation's capital and surrounding area, including Arlington National Cemetery, the nation's most revered resting ground for service men and women, and the nearby Lincoln Memorial.

Some aviation experts also raised safety concerns given its proximity to Reagan Washington National Airport. However, the Federal Aviation Administration greenlit the project in September.

The president previously justified the arch as a "military complex" to be used for drones and snipers. The new renderings indicate the arch is also now dedicated to the nation's military history.

The National Capital Planning Commission, a regional authority, voted on Thursday to approve the arch project after hearing from about 100 opponents, including Democratic lawmakers. Hours later, US District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day restraining order on construction, saying it would last about three years and "disrupt traffic, create noise, result in large-scale excavation, and more."

The Trump administration contends Congress approved the arch more than 100 years ago when it also authorized construction of a bridge across the Potomac River.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle on Friday said the federal ruling came from "an activist district court" and added, "We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch — a tribute to 250 years of American greatness."

Construction is expected to take two to three years, according to Interior Department documents submitted to the planning commission on Thursday.

Reporting by Bo Erickson; Editing by Bill Berkrot

items.title: Four things to note from Friday's US jobs report
items.content_html:
• Foreign-born workers account for all net labor force participation and employment gains since July
  • Manufacturing adds 101,000 jobs since December 2025, leaving net gain of 8,000 under Trump
  • Median and average unemployment spells are longest in about a decade excluding the pandemic
  • Information and finance remain weakest in AI-exposed industries

Nov 6 (Reuters) - The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October — 100,000 more than expected by economists — and the unemployment rate ticked down unexpectedly to 4.1% amid a fairly broad-based improvement in the job market.

Here is a look at four notable data points from the Bureau of Labor Statistics report.

FOREIGN-BORN WORKERS LEAD GAINS

The US labor force had contracted notably during President Donald Trump's first year back in office, and economists connected the large outflows of foreign-born workers that led the decline to Trump's immigration crackdown. Recently that has been reversing.

The workforce has expanded sharply in the last three months in particular, and all of the net gains in labor force participation and employment -- as measured by the payrolls report's household survey -- have come from foreign-born workers. Employment and participation among native-born workers have fallen since July.

MANUFACTURING COMEBACK

Factory work is another corner of the job market experiencing a U-turn to the upside. In Trump's first year, the manufacturing sector shed 93,000 jobs even as he imposed tariffs on imported goods to try to boost domestic factory employment.

That decline began reversing this year, and since December 2025 the sector has added 101,000 jobs, leading to a net gain of 8,000 factory jobs since Trump returned to the White House.

JOBLESS FOR LONGER

The recent uptick in the pace of hiring has not yet begun to shorten the length of time that people who lose a job are out of work. While layoffs remain subdued and job gains have been sufficient in number to lower the unemployment rate, those with the misfortune of losing a job on average are remaining out of work for longer than any time in the past five years.

Excluding the short-lived surge in unemployment during the COVID-19 pandemic, both the median and average duration of unemployment -- 11.9 weeks and 27.1 weeks, respectively -- are the longest in about a decade.

AI IMPACTS

Most economists agree that the ever-widening adoption of artificial intelligence tools by employers has yet to produce major job displacements across the economy. That doesn't mean they are entirely absent.

"The most AI-exposed sectors, information and finance, continued to struggle and have shed jobs on a trend basis," Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics, noted following the jobs report. "By contrast, professional and business services, which also has high AI adoption, bucked that trend and added 70,000 jobs in October while seeing upward revisions to past months. Those gains were broad, spanning temporary help and management and technical consulting services."

Reporting by Dan Burns; Editing by Andrea Ricci

items.title: US Senator Murphy to miss Senate votes for weeks as he recovers from stroke
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Democratic US Senator Chris Murphy said on Friday he would miss the next several weeks of votes in the Senate as he continues his recovery from a stroke.

"In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today," the Connecticut senator said in a statement.

Murphy suffered a small hemorrhagic stroke on October 31, said Jose Suarez, chief of Neurosciences Critical Care at the Johns Hopkins Hospital.

"He has shown tremendous progress, and at the current rate of improvement, we expect that he will make a full recovery following rehabilitation," Suarez said in the statement.

Reporting by Ismail Shakil and Bhargav Acharya; Editing by David Ljunggren

items.title: Trump makes hardliner Stephen Miller his chief of staff after midterm defeat
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his chief of staff on Friday, giving the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies one of the most powerful jobs in Washington after Republicans lost control of Congress.

Miller, who will replace Susie Wiles, assumes the role as the president prepares to confront a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate and a wave of congressional investigations into his administration.

A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a moment when the Republican Party's defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda.

In a social media post, Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisors," and praised Wiles for doing "an outstanding job." Trump said the change would take effect on Monday.

A White House official said Miller's appointment signals that Trump has no intention of rethinking his policies and instead is rewarding his most loyal aides.

"He's not changing course," the official said, despite tens of millions of American voters repudiating Trump's domestic agenda and foreign policy.

Trump said this week he was willing to work with Democrats on Capitol Hill. But elevating Miller, who is known for being caustic and uncompromising, could signal a more confrontational approach and a renewed push to advance the president's agenda on immigration and other issues, several White House officials said.

Trump had been displeased with his political and communications operations in the run-up to Tuesday's election as his public approval ratings fell near record lows. This week, he said the White House needed to be "more aggressive" as Democrats retake congressional power, according to a person briefed on the matter.

"The mission now is more clear than ever," Miller said on X after his appointment. "Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic."

Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to become the new Democratic speaker of the House, responded to the announcement by calling Miller a "reckless extremist" in a posting on X.

MILLER DRIVING IMMIGRATION CRACKDOWN

Miller, 41, is one of Trump's longest-serving aides and one of only a few who served throughout his first and second terms in office.

Since Trump's return to the White House in 2025, Miller has officially served as deputy chief of staff under Wiles, but he has wielded outsize influence across much of Trump's domestic agenda and has had the president's ear.

He is perhaps best known for driving Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown, setting a goal of 3,000 arrests a day. The efforts to meet that target pushed masked US immigration officers into communities around the country, increasingly arresting people with no criminal records and who had been living in the country for decades.

The crackdown, however, gets poor marks with Americans. Just 36% of respondents to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed early this week approve of it, with 54% disapproving.

Representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, said the party planned to investigate Miller's immigration policies. "Stephen Miller should lawyer up," he said.

Miller was also deeply involved in Trump's campaign to remake the federal bureaucracy, which led to the dismissal of tens of thousands of civil servants in 2025. He was also a driving force behind the administration's battles with universities, diversity programs and other institutions.

HAWKISH FOREIGN POLICY

On foreign policy, Miller has been a vocal supporter of Trump's deadly military strikes on boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean and Pacific, a campaign that has raised legal questions.

He has also praised US and Israeli strikes in Iran and defended a naval blockade and sanctions as ways to weaken Tehran and curb its ability to threaten its neighbors. It is not clear whether that is still his view after voters punished Republicans this week in part for the economic fallout from the Iran war.

Marc Short, who was chief of staff to then-Vice President Mike Pence in Trump's first term, said that in Miller, Trump is "getting someone who is wed to him" and who is willing to battle Congress over issues like immigration and congressional investigations.

"It would not suggest that there is high expectation for bipartisan legislation," Short said in an interview.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who faces Democratic calls for impeachment over the Iran war, celebrated Miller's promotion with a social media post reading, "Patriots in control," reflecting the enthusiasm of some Trump allies for putting Miller in a position of greater authority.

SHAKE UP AFTER ELECTION SETBACK

The chief of staff typically wields great influence as the president's gatekeeper. The person manages White House staff, organizes the president's time and schedule, and oversees other government departments and lawmakers.

Wiles, 69, who submitted her resignation on Thursday night, will move to Trump's political operation, according to a White House official.

The veteran political operative from Florida was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff.

She brought decades of political experience to the role and was regarded as running a more disciplined operation than some of Trump's prior top aides. She maintained her role even while undergoing treatment earlier this year for early-stage breast cancer.

Wiles rarely challenged Trump's policies but brought discipline to an often chaotic operation and was seen as a voice of reason. Her exit raises questions about who will play her role.

Trump ran through four chiefs of staff – an unusually high number – during his 2017-2021 term, as they were seen to have struggled to rein in the unpredictable president.

items.title: Jay Rockefeller, heir to famed dynasty and healthcare advocate in US Senate, dies at 89
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - John D. "Jay" Rockefeller IV, the progeny of one of America's most famous and wealthiest families who during three decades in the US Senate sought expanded healthcare for the poor and excoriated President George W. Bush's handling of the Iraq war, died aged 89 on Friday at his home in Washington, his wife Sharon Percy Rockefeller said.

She added that plans were underway for a service at the Washington National Cathedral.

Rockefeller, a tall, soft-spoken Democrat with liberal views, was elected in 1984 to the first of his five six-year terms representing West Virginia in the Senate after two terms as governor of the poor coal-mining state.

Rockefeller voted in 2002 in favor of the Republican Bush's measure authorizing the Iraq war, which began with a US-led invasion in 2003. He later expressed regret over that vote and, as head of the Senate intelligence committee, accused Bush of taking the nation to war on "false premises."

He was a great-grandson of oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller and the scion of a family that formed a political dynasty that included his uncle, New York Governor Nelson Rockefeller.

New York-born Jay Rockefeller's life changed direction after he graduated from Harvard and served in a national service program in impoverished rural West Virginia from 1964 to 1966.

When he was put in public office, he worked to increase healthcare access, fight poverty, provide health benefits to coal miners and assist military veterans. As a senator, he had a role in shaping the program created in 1997 under which the US government helps states provide medical coverage for millions of uninsured children.

Rockefeller backed Democratic President Bill Clinton's failed proposal for near-universal health insurance coverage in the 1990s and then fought for Democratic President Barack Obama's successful quest for a healthcare overhaul law, signed in 2010.

In the debate over Obama's measure, Rockefeller unsuccessfully sought to have the federal government offer a medical insurance program to the general population — in addition to existing programs for the poor and elderly — as an alternative to private insurance plans that could be costly and exclusive.

"Championing those most in need has been my life's calling and I will never stop fighting to make a difference for the people who mean so much to me," Rockefeller said in 2013 when he announced at age 75 he would not seek a sixth Senate term.

Before the Iraq invasion, Bush's administration built the case for war by touting intelligence indicating Iraq owned an arsenal of weapons of mass destruction — they actually did not exist — and alleged ties between Iraqi leaders and the al Qaeda network responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US.

"If I had known then what I know now, I would have voted against it," Rockefeller told the Charleston Gazette newspaper in 2004, referring to the 2002 war authorization measure.

"I think the intelligence was shaped," he continued. "And I think the interpretation of the intelligence was shaped. You had a president who we now know was determined to go to war."

'FUNDAMENTALLY MISLEADING'

A report from the intelligence committee issued in 2008, when he served as its chairman, asserted that Bush, Vice President Dick Cheney and other leading officials exaggerated intelligence findings and ignored disputes within US intelligence circles about Iraq's weapons and the hotly disputed ties to al Qaeda.

The report rejected pre-war statements by Bush and Cheney that Iraq might give al Qaeda weapons of mass destruction.

"Representing to the American people that the two had an operational partnership and posed a single, indistinguishable threat was fundamentally misleading and led the nation to war on false premises," Rockefeller said as the report was released.

During his Senate tenure, he also headed the Commerce, Science, and Transportation and Veterans Affairs committees.

Rockefeller was born on June 18, 1937, weeks after the death of his great-grandfather, who had been America's richest man.

The Rockefeller name came with high expectations. His father was a famous philanthropist. His uncle Nelson served as US vice president, as well as governor of New York. His uncle David Rockefeller headed Chase Manhattan Bank and uncle Winthrop Rockefeller was governor of Arkansas.

He was elected to West Virginia's legislature in 1966 before age 30, then elected West Virginia's secretary of state in 1968.

He lost a bid to become governor in 1972, then served as a college president before being elected governor in 1976. Rockefeller, who became one of the wealthiest members of the US Congress, spent millions of dollars of his own money to bankroll his successful campaign for the US Senate in 1984.

Rockefeller sometimes found himself overshadowed by his state's other senator, Robert Byrd, who died in 2010 at age 92 as the longest-serving member of Congress in US history.

He usually backed his state's coal and steel industries but angered coal executives in 2012 by fighting Republican efforts to prevent regulation of emissions from coal-fired power plants.

He was married to public television executive Sharon Percy Rockefeller, with whom he had four children.

Technology shares sold off dramatically on Thursday on growing concerns that a new Congress controlled by Democrats will slow artificial intelligence development, and fears that the massive capital expenditure on building out AI will not yield sufficient returns. The meeting on Friday was scheduled to convene the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, an outside panel that advises President Donald Trump. The group also includes AMD CEO Lisa Su, Oracle Chief Technology Officer Larry Ellison and Marc Andreessen, the co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz. Its co-chairs are venture capitalist David Sacks and White House tech adviser Michael Kratsios.

The Energy Department's meeting website briefly listed November 13 as the new date for the meeting, but the agency later sent an email retracting that.

The initial meeting announcement said the panel would advise Trump's new AI task force, dubbed the "Super Intelligence Task Force," which includes cabinet officials, Trump appointees and White House staff. Super intelligence is the president's preferred term for AI.

items.title: US prosecutor who oversaw probes into past Trump investigations resigns
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Jason Reding Quiñones, who oversaw probes into past criminal investigations of US President Donald Trump as the top federal prosecutor in Miami, has resigned, Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Friday.

As US attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Quiñones was at the center of Trump's attempts to leverage the Justice Department to exact revenge on his political adversaries. His office was tasked with investigating the criminal probes of Trump's handling of classified documents after he left office in 2021 and his campaign's contacts with Russia in the 2016 election, among other issues. Those efforts have not borne fruit so far.

His resignation marks the departure of the second senior Justice Department official since Tuesday's midterm elections, when Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress. The DOJ now is without leaders for two of its signature initiatives — relitigating past investigations and targeting higher education. Harmeet Dhillon, who headed the DOJ's civil-rights unit, resigned on Thursday.

It was not immediately clear why Quiñones resigned. In a statement on X, Quiñones said his resignation was effective Friday and called it an honor to serve in the role.

His office had also brought criminal charges against former Cuban President Raul Castro in a major escalation of the Trump administration's pressure campaign against the communist country.

items.title: US inflation too high; essential to get back to 2%: Fed's Williams
items.content_html:
FRANKFURT, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US economic growth has remained resilient and the labour market is remarkably stable despite successive shocks, but inflation is too high and must be brought back to 2%, New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Friday.

Inflation has soared across the world, mostly as the US war on Iran has pushed energy prices higher but also because soaring investment in AI has pushed up costs for some IT-related products and services.

"Inflation is absolutely too high. It's been too high for too long," Williams told a European Central Bank conference in Frankfurt. "It's absolutely essential that we bring inflation back to our 2% target in a timely manner and a sustained basis."

But Williams also argued that the Fed's key focus should be on where inflation is heading and making sure that current shocks do not translate into broader or more persistent inflation.

"Fortunately, we're not seeing that happen so far in terms of inflation expectations, which remain well anchored," Williams said. "We're seeing wage growth (that is), I think, consistent with our 2% goal."

While Williams did not discuss what the Fed's next policy move should be, he said the bank's last policy statement had correctly concluded that it was appropriate for the Fed to collect more information to determine what the appropriate stance of policy is.

Financial markets see a more than 50% chance of a rate hike by the Fed in December while a move by March is fully priced in.

Reporting by Francesco Canepa; writing by Balazs Koranyi; editing by Gareth Jones

items.title: Trump takes action to make sure the Oval Office stays oval
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Even as he puts his golden imprint on the White House, President Donald Trump moved on Thursday to protect two of its most historic spaces, the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, from major modifications by future presidents.

Trump signed a proclamation that he said would be the first step toward declaring the West Wing spaces as a national monument to mark their place in American history.

It was unclear what exactly led Trump to seek protection of the structures from Congress now. There has been no move to tear down or dramatically alter the spaces.

The proclamation notes that the White House is already recognized as a national historic landmark but "nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance." Trump said his proclamation would need congressional approval.

"So if they want to say 'let's not have Oval anymore, let's make it square,' what happens is they have to go back to Congress, and hopefully the Congress... will be smart enough not to let that happen," Trump said.

The action came two days after midterm elections that cost Republicans control of Congress. Democrats will assume the majority in January, curtailing Trump's legislative influence in the final years of his presidency.

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has transformed the Oval Office with gold accents, paved over the Rose Garden, torn down the East Wing to make way for a ballroom, resurfaced the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and more.

The changes have faced opposition and in some cases court challenges, but nothing thus far has dissuaded the president.

Environmental groups criticized Trump after he signed orders in July slashing the size of two national monuments in southern Utah by more than 90% to allow for grazing, motorized recreation, logging and other resource development in the region.

Trump's signing ceremony on Thursday marked the third time this week he had promoted his pet projects. On Monday, in what was billed as his closing argument to voters ahead of the Tuesday elections, he unveiled his refurbished Reflecting Pool. On Wednesday, the day after Republicans' election rout, he gave reporters a tour of the ballroom construction.

Trump cited the history of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as the reason for needing to protect them. Both locations are the sites of major international and domestic meetings and both have been in the same locations since the 1930s.

In a nod to the looming change in control of Congress, a red hat that said VETO sat on Trump's desk during the signing of the proclamation.

As reporters were led to the Cabinet room for a quick tour, Trump was asked if the next president would be allowed to take down all his gold decorations.

"They can do anything they want," Trump said, "as long as they do it carefully."

Reporting By Steve Holland; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Stephen Coates

items.title: Texas governor-elect says state will have laws to shield citizens from data centers
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state will introduce laws to protect its residents with regards to data centers, citing their impact on rural communities.

With plentiful energy supplies, relatively cheap land and a pro-business policy, Texas has become one of the leading regions in the world for data center developments.

"Data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans," Democrat Hinojosa, who beat Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in Tuesday's election, told CNN in an interview.

"We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections," she said, adding that communities should have "a seat at the table" on if and how data centers operate in their areas.

US President Donald Trump's administration has strongly backed data center expansion as a national priority, but the public is increasingly opposed to such projects, citing concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, wildlife impacts and public access to federal lands.

Abbott became one of the first Republican governors in the US to halt the connection of new data centers to the state's electric grid and ordered a comprehensive audit of the projects.

Hinojosa has rattled the state's data center industry with a campaign pledge to halt new projects.

Billionaire Elon Musk supported Abbott in the election and had spent $158 million to promote Texas Republican US Senate candidate Ken Paxton alone, Musk said on Wednesday.

Musk's SpaceX (SPCX.O) and Tesla (TSLA.O) are headquartered in the Lone Star State, where he is also planning a chipmaking venture.

Texas can also have a strong working relationship with Musk and his companies, but on her administration's terms, Hinojosa added.

In October, publication Texas Monthly reported that the state had been discussing the sale of Boca Chica State Park to SpaceX, citing sources.

During a news conference on Thursday, Hinojosa said she had spoken to the executive director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission "to request that no action be taken" while there is an ongoing transition from Abbott to her.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

items.title: Midterms upended Congress but Trump still commands foreign policy
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The Republican Party's staggering losses at the ballot box this week have left President Donald Trump diminished in Washington and facing tougher legislative oversight and scrutiny of his agenda.

But on foreign policy, he could remain unbowed.

Even as Democratic lawmakers seek to rein in the Republican president when they take control of Congress, Trump will retain broad latitude to pursue his objectives on the world stage, from Iran and Israel to Ukraine and China, during his final two years in office.

The central question, analysts say, is whether Trump will feel chastened by his party's poor showing in Tuesday's midterm elections or emboldened to take more dramatic steps to craft his legacy in US relations with friends and foes alike.

Most urgent is the intractable war against Iran, which Trump acknowledged on Wednesday contributed to his party losing both chambers of Congress. He insisted, though, he had no regrets about attacking the Islamic Republic and it was essential to stop Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, which it says it has never sought.

The midterms outcome illustrated voter backlash after eight months of conflict that have driven US gasoline prices up and his approval ratings down.

Democrats had accused Republicans of ceding Congress' war-making powers and giving Trump a free hand internationally, not just against Iran but with his approach to Russia's war in Ukraine, his tariffs campaign, his capture of Venezuela's president, and deadly boat strikes off Latin America.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer told reporters on Wednesday his party's mandate is to put a check on "Trump's chaos at home and abroad" and end the Iran war.

That is easier said than done, given the extensive leeway with foreign policy and military operations that presidents have long possessed.

"A Democratic Congress has the ability to stop Trump's domestic legislative agenda, but it doesn't have much ability to stop a president from exercising his powers as commander-in-chief," said William Wechsler, senior director of Middle East programs at the Atlantic Council.

Democrats' main tools could be investigations, Trump nominees' confirmation hearings and funding authority to curb his foreign operations, but analysts say their leverage will be limited.

While not responding directly to Reuters' questions about the election's implications, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said: "President Trump has effectively restored American strength on the global stage ... The president will continue to work with anyone to put America first and improve the livelihoods of families across the country, and his foreign policy decisions have never been motivated by politics."

FACING LAME-DUCK STATUS

Presidents entering their lame-duck phase, when barred from running again and seeing influence waning at home, have often focused on global affairs – and many analysts expect something similar from Trump.

But some experts see the risk of Trump's impulsiveness leading to further instability in the Middle East or sparking conflict elsewhere, possibly targeting Cuba, a Communist-ruled island he has placed under an oil blockade and repeatedly threatened.

"If triggered and cornered," said Laura Blumenfeld, a foreign policy analyst at Johns Hopkins University, "Trump may elect to flex his presidential powers through unilateral use of force abroad."

With Iran, Trump faces the choice of launching a new round of airstrikes, seeking a negotiated exit or maintaining the status quo - a tense stalemate keeping global energy prices high and Gulf neighbors on edge.

While Iranian leaders have gloated over what they see as Trump's humiliation at home, people in Washington familiar with the deliberations say he could still take military action. One source said Trump had nothing to lose politically now.

But Sina Toossi, an Iran specialist at the Center for International Policy in Washington, said: "Escalation offers no clear path to victory and risks compounding the very economic grievances that drove voters to punish Republicans."

And any return to major hostilities could also stir further dissent within Trump's MAGA movement, where a growing number of followers are upset about him breaking his 2024 campaign promise to avoid foreign interventions.

Vice President JD Vance distanced himself from Trump's Iran policy on Wednesday, questioning whether it was worth the cost and blaming it for Republicans' electoral wipeout.

DEMOCRATS TARGET UKRAINE, ISRAEL POLICIES

Taking control of Congress in January, Democrats will also seek to revive support for Ukraine, under pressure from Trump as it fights a 4-1/2-year-old Russian invasion.

Democrats hope to draw more Republicans into efforts to approve new aid to Ukraine and build a majority that could withstand a veto by Trump, who has halted direct assistance.

Trump's lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports prompted criticism, including from some Republicans, for reinforcing the impression that he was increasingly siding with Moscow.

At the same time, Democrats want to use their newfound power to start repairing relations with European allies as well as Canada, though analysts say lawmakers alone won't be able to regain trust with governments rattled by Trump's tariffs and pressure tactics.

Trump is also expected to face a Congress less supportive of Israel than ever before, while some Republicans are also questioning their party's traditional backing for Washington's closest Middle East ally.

Many winning Democratic candidates were progressives who campaigned against military aid to Israel and the US-Israeli war on Iran, and they plan to push for an end to billions of dollars in annual assistance.

Trump himself announced on Election Day that such aid would be stopped at the end of the year - though it was not clear he has the legal authority.

Israel's military campaign in Gaza, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's embrace of Trump and the Republican Party and a wave of settler violence in the occupied West Bank had already eroded decades of bipartisan support.

Despite that, Trump's veto power could limit the Democrats' ability to force major policy changes.

In the end, most analysts see Trump's foreign policy for the remainder of his second term driven by his vision of his place in history, which so far has been based heavily on the exercise of military power abroad.

"He's concerned about his legacy of having left an imprint on the world, not necessarily a positive imprint," Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said on a webcast by the Washington think tank.

Reporting by Matt Spetalnick; Editing by Don Durfee and Daniel Wallis

items.title: Latinos, motivated by immigration and economic woes, drive Democratic gains in Republican strongholds
items.content_html:
FORT WORTH, TEXAS, Nov 5 (Reuters) - When Geronimo Perez pulled up to vote at the Worth Heights Community Center in South Fort Worth, Texas, one thing was on his mind: a friend who had been deported just a week earlier.

Perez, 56, cast his ballot for the entire Democratic ticket in this year's midterm elections. He lamented the high cost of living, but said President Donald Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement agenda drove him to support Democratic state representatives Gina Hinojosa for governor and James Talarico for US Senate.

"I represented my family, my culture," said Perez. "The United States is made up of immigrants of different colors."

Perez's vote reflected a broader shift among millions of Latino voters across the country, from the border counties of Texas and the meatpacking towns of southwest Kansas to Miami-Dade, Colorado and Arizona. After helping fuel Republican gains in recent elections, many swung back toward Democrats.

Affordability remained a major concern, but outside polling places on Election Day immigration was mentioned repeatedly in Reuters interviews with Latino voters.

Nationally, however, the economy remained the dominant issue among Hispanic voters. In exit polling conducted by SSRS, 45% named the economy as the country's top issue. Nearly 65% of Latinos voted for US House candidates, according to the data.

Additionally, record numbers of Latinos voted nationwide, reaching as many as 14.5 million, said Janet Murguía, CEO of UnidosUS, the largest US Latino civil rights organization.

"Latino voters sent a clear message about their anger and concern about the direction of our country," she said.

That shift among Latino voters was part of a broader multiracial coalition that propelled Democrats back to power, helping the party capture both chambers of Congress in victories stretching from coast to coast.

Across the 64 majority-Latino counties with Senate races that were mostly counted, Republicans lost 14 points off their 2024 share, outpacing national trends, according to a Reuters analysis of county-level voting trends. In Hidalgo County, Texas, support for Republicans dropped about 25 points, and in Miami-Dade, Florida — a county Trump won in 2024 — it fell 10 points.

Nowhere was that picture clearer than in Texas, where Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who has served in Texas state politics for more than 30 years. Yet, Hinojosa's "Latino voter strategy" was simple: Treat the electorate, one of the swingiest in the country, as if they're no different from non-Latino voters.

She defeated Abbott by about 6.5 percentage points, 52.5% to 46%, according to the most recent vote totals.

Her message to Latino Texans would be the same as to non-Latinos — she would just say it in Spanish, she told Reuters in January. And in an interview at her Austin-based campaign headquarters in July, she said it shouldn't be odd to have a Latina as governor of Texas.

She won't be alone: Democrat Xavier Becerra, who was health and human services secretary under President Joe Biden, won his gubernatorial race in California. It will be the first time in modern history that the two most populous states, California and Texas, will both be led by Latino governors at the same time.

In Texas, Talarico made an effort to engage with Latino voters across the state throughout his campaign, said Daniel Alegre, CEO of Spanish-language media giant TelevisaUnivision. He said that was one of the keys to Talarico's victory.

"It's up to the campaigns to realize this and not fall into 2014 or 2016 methodology; that doesn't work anymore," he said.

RAIDS HELP DRIVE VOTER REGISTRATIONS

In southwest Kansas, three solidly red counties turned blue in the US Senate race following ICE raids on towns dominated by meatpacking plants staffed by a largely immigrant workforce.

ICE agents descended on Ford, Finney and Seward counties in September for an operation that detained more than 100 people, state officials said.

The raids slowed operations at plants and delayed shipments of thousands of cattle, according to livestock associations, at a time of record high beef prices in the United States.

When Reuters visited a week after the raids, local organizers had seized the moment and, as a result, those three counties saw among the five highest increases in voter registrations in the state, according to data from the IKE Lab, a research project of Wichita State University.

"You can tell people are angry," said Angelica Plata, a community organizer with New Frontiers, a local non-profit focused on racial and economic inequities.

That anger has been palpable all year, said Beatriz Lopez, executive director of Voto Latino, a national organization that works to register and mobilize Latino voters.

The next challenge, she said, is to not take this electorate for granted, because no party has a hold on Latinos.

"If they want to in 2028, if they want to sustain this momentum, if they want these big wins, invest in us, invest in the Latino vote."

Reporting by David Hood-Nuño; Editing by Kat Stafford and Daniel Wallis

items.title: Trump ally Dhillon, who remade DOJ civil rights unit, resigns
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - US Justice Department official Harmeet Dhillon, who reshaped the agency's civil rights unit to pursue Trump administration priorities including voter data requests and gun rights cases, has resigned, Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday.

Dhillon is among the first senior officials to leave the administration after Tuesday's midterm elections, in which Democrats retook both chambers of Congress.

Dhillon, a Trump ally, oversaw an overhaul of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, which has historically enforced laws protecting voting rights and fighting racial discrimination. Under her leadership, the division shifted focus toward challenging diversity initiatives and investigating antisemitism on college campuses, leading to probes of several elite universities.

The changes prompted a wave of departures among career staff. Dhillon said attorneys in the unit pursued liberal priorities and were unwilling to implement Trump's agenda.

In a resignation letter, Dhillon cited as accomplishments efforts to force US institutions to scale back diversity initiatives and challenges to school districts over transgender policies. She said she told the White House in October she planned to resign.

"We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls' sports, and so much more," Dhillon posted on social media, thanking Trump for the appointment.

She will return to her law firm, The Dhillon Law Group, according to her spokesperson. Her firm had recently shrunk as some attorneys left for other practices.

Two people familiar with the matter said Dhillon was frustrated that she had been passed over for promotions in the department and wanted to return to her firm to reinvigorate it.

The Civil Rights Division in prior administrations conducted investigations into police departments accused of systematic civil rights violations, including after high-profile killings of Black people by local police.

"For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded," said Stacey Young, the head of Justice Connection, an advocacy group. "Dhillon decimated it."

Dhillon withdrew earlier findings from those police probes and investigated whether some Democratic-led cities violated people's gun rights under the Second Amendment to the US Constitution.

TARGETING UNIVERSITIES

Dhillon led investigations to pressure dozens of universities she viewed as too liberal. Many of those centered on alleged antisemitism, diversity initiatives, and treatment of transgender people.

Those probes helped the department extract hundreds of millions of dollars in settlement agreements from some of the nation's premier universities, and even led to the resignation of the president of the University of Virginia. One high-profile target, Harvard University, refused to pay a large settlement and instead has repeatedly fought the Trump administration in court.

Ahead of the midterms, the division played a major role in the Trump administration's efforts to prevent noncitizens from voting, a phenomenon that independent reviews have found is exceedingly rare. The DOJ lost a series of cases to obtain private voter data from states and deployed about 1,000 staff to monitor polling sites during Tuesday's vote.

Dhillon has also been involved in cases against perceived Trump enemies.

The civil rights unit brought a high-profile criminal case against former CNN anchor Don Lemon and others accused of disrupting a church service in January to protest the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Minnesota.

The division also sought unsuccessfully to bring criminal charges against Cassidy Hutchinson, a former White House aide who gave vivid testimony to Congress about Trump's actions on the day of the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot.

items.title: Google plans $17 billion Wyoming data center amid rising threats of curbs
items.content_html:
Nov 5 (Reuters) - Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google will invest $17 billion to build its first data center in Wyoming, the company said on Thursday, pushing ahead with a major AI infrastructure investment as political resistance to data center expansion grows following the US midterm elections.

Of the 41 data center-related ballot measures voted on this week, all but one went against data centers, according to Ballotpedia.

Google's facility will be built in partnership with Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power (AEP.O) and Related Digital.

The project will be powered in part by a planned 702-megawatt fuel-cell development equipped with carbon capture and storage technology. The fuel cells will be supplied by Bloom Energy (BE.N).

Wyoming is a Republican stronghold, where Donald Trump won more than 70% of the presidential vote in 2024.

The announcement comes as investors reassess the pace of the AI infrastructure buildout. Wins by candidates opposed to data-center expansion in key Texas and Georgia races during the midterm elections have added to concerns that political resistance could complicate the industry's rapid expansion.

Meanwhile, Microsoft (MSFT.O) has declined to expand a Texas data-center agreement with AI cloud provider Nscale, with Bloomberg News reporting earlier in the day that the company planned to tighten oversight of some data-center projects from neocloud providers Nebius, IREN and Nscale.

Shares of Bloom Energy also slumped more than 14% on worries that any potential restrictions could hit the industry.

Reporting by Prathik Jayaprakash in Bengaluru; Editing by Sriraj Kalluvila

items.title: Democrats won Congress, but can they meet voters' demands?
items.content_html:
Nov 5 (Reuters) - Democrats had an extraordinary night on Tuesday. They routed Republicans, sweeping President Donald Trump's party from power on Capitol Hill. But does recapturing both chambers of Congress mean Democrats have a mandate to govern - and will Trump let them?

I have been speaking to strategists in both parties this week, and they warn that despite the scale of the victory, it was more a resounding repudiation of Donald Trump and his failure to lower prices than a blank check for the Democratic agenda.

Democrats may soon discover that winning the midterms was the easy part. Despite the Democrats recapturing Congress, Trump retains veto power, and Democrats have yet to articulate a viable plan to address voters' concerns. They could soon find themselves accountable for the economic frustrations that swept them back into power.

Voters angry about the cost of food, gas and housing, exacerbated by the Iran war and Trump's tariffs on foreign goods, are impatient for change. But Democrats have little power to lower prices, because many of the forces driving inflation are outside Congress' control.

The likeliest outcome in Washington in the next two years will be legislative gridlock.

Trump still holds significant executive power, including over tariff policy and military operations, although Democrats have said they will seek to limit funding for the Iran conflict. He can bypass Congress on a range of major issues, including immigration enforcement, foreign policy, federal regulations and trade.

Democrats will likely pass measures aimed at lowering costs, many of which could face a veto from Trump. The moves would allow Democrats to argue they are trying to address voters' economic concerns as the party prepares for the 2028 presidential election, but real change could be elusive.

Trump largely ignored Congress after taking office in 2025, and White House aides say he will continue to push his agenda through executive actions in his last two years in office, especially now that Democrats control Capitol Hill.

While Trump has said he is willing to work with Democrats, he is unlikely to hand them major legislative victories ahead of the 2028 election, when the country will choose his successor. He has already signaled his willingness to use his veto.

Democrats will be able to block Trump's appointments, including to the US Supreme Court, while pursuing corruption investigations of Trump, his allies and his administration. Expect a blizzard of subpoenas and document requests.

An influx of young progressives into Congress could increase pressure on party leaders to impeach Trump, although Democrats do not have enough votes in the Senate to remove him from office. Some Democrats worry such proceedings could backfire politically as voters want the party laser-focused on the cost of living.

Trump emerges from the midterms politically weakened, with members of his own party already distancing themselves from him as they look ahead to 2028. But Trump retains significant power and should not be underestimated.

  • Latinos, motivated by immigration and economic woes, drive Democratic gains in Republican strongholds

  • How Democrats expanded the map and won rural America
  • Democratic victories bring historic breakthroughs for women and minorities

THE VIEW FROM ABROAD

World leaders reacted swiftly to Democrats winning the midterm elections, a result that could have major implications for global trade, security and energy prices. Most welcomed the result, signaling their unhappiness with Trump and his foreign policy agenda, which has upended international relations, especially inside the NATO alliance.
